missing_spec_content.spec_text: Students should be able to explain ways of reducing unwanted energy transfers, for example through lubrication and the use of thermal insulation.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson says energy is wasted but never explains how to reduce unwanted transfers. Lubrication and thermal insulation are not mentioned anywhere.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: The higher the thermal conductivity of a material the higher the rate of energy transfer by conduction across the material.
missing_spec_content.why: Thermal conductivity is not mentioned. Conduction appears only as a word in brackets, with no link to rate of energy transfer.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Students should be able to describe how the rate of cooling of a building is affected by the thickness and thermal conductivity of its walls.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson does not cover how wall thickness and thermal conductivity affect how fast a building cools.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Required practical activity 2 (physics only): investigate the effectiveness of different materials as thermal insulators and the factors that may affect the thermal insulation properties of a material.
missing_spec_content.why: The required practical on thermal insulators is not covered.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: (HT only) Students should be able to describe ways to increase the efficiency of an intended energy transfer.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson defines and calculates efficiency but gives no ways to increase it.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Throughout this section on Energy students should be able to calculate the changes in energy involved when a system is changed by: heating, work done by forces, work done when a current flows
missing_spec_content.why: No energy-change calculation is taught for heating, work done by forces or work done when a current flows. The only numerical work is the lamp Sankey example and the efficiency checkpoint. The Ek, Ep and Ee equations appear only inside keyTerms definitions and are never applied.

factual_errors.text: A perfect device would have efficiency = 1.0 (or 100%). In reality it is always less, because some energy is always dissipated.
factual_errors.correction: This is true for most devices. But where the intended output is heating the surroundings, as in an electric heater, the 'dissipated' thermal energy is the useful output, so efficiency can be effectively 100%. The lesson should say 'for most devices' or 'almost always'. The same absolute claim appears in revisionCardBullets[7] ('Efficiency is always less than 1.0 (100%). Some energy is always dissipated') and in keyPoints[4].memTip ('It is always less than 1').

wrong_terms.text: The pathway is mechanically, electrically, by heating or by radiation. This wording earns marks.
wrong_terms.spec_term: The specification names the ways a system is changed as 'heating', 'work done by forces' and 'work done when a current flows' (4.1.1.1). 'Mechanically' and 'electrically' are not specification terms. 'By radiation' is not among the ways listed in these sections. The claim that this exact wording earns marks is not supported by the specification text.

wrong_terms.text: MEHR: Mechanical, Electrical, Heating, Radiation. These are the four transfer pathways examiners expect.
wrong_terms.spec_term: 'work done by forces', 'work done when a current flows', 'heating' (4.1.1.1). The specification sections list three ways, not four named pathways.

wrong_terms.text: Mechanically. The friction force between the brakes and wheels does work to slow the car
